The held passage describes a Q2 2026 launch plan. This pilot has not verified completion, availability, uptake or commercial terms; it must not be presented as a realised integration.
A dated launch confirmation and usage evidence would move this from planned distribution to observed operation.

P-09.direction_note: Direction identifies the specified mechanism; it does not assert one-way influence across the entire relationship.

segments.text: One analyst estimates that Harvey and Legora meet in most enterprise procurements at major firms and portrays their backers as rival camps; held funding reporting also names investors appearing on both sides. Legora’s CEO forecasts that the leader will take 90% of the market.

Analyst inference: The vendors seek the same enterprise workflow budgets. Investments in implementation and customer relationships may help each win a central place in a firm’s work, while their multiple-model strategies compete above rather than solely at the model layer.

The claim about most procurements is one analyst’s estimate. Legora’s CEO’s winner-takes-most prediction is self-interested and is not a market-share finding. Multi-vendor purchasing remains a competing possibility. Investor portfolios overlap; the evidence does not establish exclusive or coordinated camps.
Independently observed win/loss patterns, renewal and firms standardising on one vendor would strengthen concentration; enduring multi-vendor use would weaken it.

P-10.direction_note: Direction identifies the specified mechanism; it does not assert one-way influence across the entire relationship.

segments.text: Most surveyed in-house respondents see an opportunity to insource drafting, contracts and research, and nearly two-thirds (64%) expect to rely less on outside counsel, a figure the report does not tie clearly to the US or the full sample; Ford's GC says Ford is likely to expand work with fast-moving firms and curtail reliance on laggards; buyers say rate hikes continue with little explanation of AI investment.

Analyst inference: Legal departments can condition allocation of matters on delivery and price, and can consider producing some work themselves. Firms still contribute specialised expertise, while both sides must translate efficiency into an agreed way to pay for it.

Survey intentions and one general counsel’s statement do not establish widespread spending changes. The buyer class is heterogeneous; neither Ford’s statement nor vendor-co-published survey findings apply automatically to every buyer or firm.
Observed changes to matter allocation or fee terms would strengthen the reading; unchanged purchasing despite dissatisfaction would weaken it.

P-11.direction_note: Direction identifies the specified mechanism; it does not assert one-way influence across the entire relationship.

segments.text: Harvey reports over 500 in-house legal teams as customers and names Bridgewater, Comcast and Carvana — vendor self-report.

Analyst inference: In-house teams are potential direct purchasers, widening Harvey’s route to legal work beyond selling to law firms. Direct access to a buyer’s workflow could change who captures efficiency gains, but the choice to insource still rests with the buyer.

Customer names and reach are vendor self-report. They do not establish realised savings, displaced firm revenue or a contract with Ford. A direct software purchase may complement outside advice rather than replace it.
Documented in-house use replacing externally purchased tasks would strengthen the substitution mechanism; use to coordinate outside counsel would support complementarity.

P-12.direction_note: Direction identifies the specified mechanism; it does not assert one-way influence across the entire relationship.

segments.text: One aggregator analysis reports over 60% of carriers asking AI questions at renewal; a broker says insurers may impose warranties on AI use or certified tools, many insurers will expect evidence of adaptation, and sanctions are generally not covered. On the analysis's reading, coverage conditions steer firm practice.

Analyst inference: A carrier’s request for governance and verification evidence can make insurance renewal a route through which AI controls enter firm practice. The leverage depends on the importance of coverage and available alternatives, not on insurers appearing frequently in the corpus.

This gatekeeping effect is an inference. Much 2026 detail comes from one unverified aggregator; Lockton describes possible warranties, and sanctions being generally uncovered does not establish universal exclusion of AI-related negligence.
Verified carrier forms, renewal conditions and loss experience would strengthen or revise this account; readily available alternative cover could limit the leverage.

P-13.direction_note: Direction identifies the specified mechanism; it does not assert one-way influence across the entire relationship.

segments.text: Freshfields cited a changing market and technology investment when beginning paralegal redundancies; the held report describes staff and reader interpretations linking this to AI. Other sources describe Ropes & Gray’s encouragement of first-year AI training, flat AmLaw 200 entry-level hiring and MinterEllison’s publicly AI-linked graduate-intake cut. These are distinct firm and market examples, not one uniform causal finding.

Analyst inference: Firms allocate junior work and training while relying on junior labour for parts of production. AI can therefore affect both immediate staffing economics and the work through which future expertise develops; authority over intake is more concentrated than the consequences.

The evidence covers different firms and does not establish a uniform policy. Flat hiring does not identify AI as its cause; MinterEllison’s attributed cut and Ropes & Gray’s training initiative support different responses. The Freshfields AI attribution includes anonymous staff commentary, rather than an explicit firm statement identifying AI as the cause.
Evidence of changed task allocation and training outcomes alongside hiring would clarify whether AI removes learning opportunities or redesigns them.

P-14.direction_note: Direction identifies the specified mechanism; it does not assert one-way influence across the entire relationship.

segments.text: Freshfields integrates Claude into proprietary platforms connected to institutional knowledge, and Anthea Roberts and David B. Wilkins, The Scrambled Competitive Map reports it live with 5,700 users on launch day.

Analyst inference: Direct integration lets a firm combine model capability with institutional knowledge and proprietary tools. This gives the model provider a route to firms that does not necessarily run through a separate legal-AI application vendor.

The named example is Freshfields, not every large firm. Roberts–Wilkins report launch use; firm statements describe integration. Neither establishes independent productivity gains or a supply contract for Kirkland or A&O Shearman.
Repeatable evidence of direct firm deployments and vendor substitution would strengthen the bypass mechanism; continued reliance on specialist workflow suppliers would limit it.

P-15.direction_note: Direction identifies the specified mechanism; it does not assert one-way influence across the entire relationship.

segments.text: Firms build proprietary AI in a strategy that could help mitigate the vendor threat, including Kirkland's $500 million build; in Anthea Roberts and David B. Wilkins, Harvey's Strategic Evolution, the intermediation layer is increasingly optional for firms with engineering capability.

Analyst inference: Internal engineering can create an alternative to parts of a vendor’s workflow layer. Roberts–Wilkins argue that intermediation becomes increasingly optional for firms with that capability; the implication is conditional on capability, usable data and implementation.

This is potential substitution, not observed hostility or a class-wide decision to leave Harvey. Kirkland’s simultaneous build and buy strategy demonstrates why internal development alone does not prove vendor displacement.
Measured replacement of vendor workflows would strengthen the mechanism; increased vendor purchasing alongside internal builds would support complementarity.

P-16.direction_note: Direction identifies the specified mechanism; it does not assert one-way influence across the entire relationship.

segments.text: Legora serves White & Case, HSFK, Linklaters and corporate legal departments such as Barclays, lets firms deploy client-facing workspaces under their own brand, and partners with Kirkland & Ellis.

Analyst inference: Legora supplies tools firms can use internally and through client-facing workspaces. Firms can retain a branded client interface while drawing on vendor capability, creating interdependence over delivery even when the client sees the firm’s name.
Named customers and platform capabilities do not show that every customer uses every feature. A group supplier relationship is not a licence to attach an inferred Legora edge to each large firm.
Evidence of sustained client-workspace adoption would strengthen the delivery role; narrow internal experimentation would support a smaller interpretation.

P-17.direction_note: Direction identifies the specified mechanism; it does not assert one-way influence across the entire relationship.

segments.text: Legora is built primarily on Claude; Harvey, Legora, Eve, Crosby and Solve Intelligence all build on Claude.

Analyst inference: Legora’s reliance on Claude makes Anthropic an upstream supplier of a key capability. Legora must add workflow, integration and customer value beyond access to that model if the underlying provider also supplies legal features.

Descriptions of the stack do not establish exclusive contractual dependence, usage shares or inability to substitute another model. The claim is based on commentary rather than an audited architecture.
Confirmed architecture, switching costs and changes in model routing would determine the depth of dependency.

P-18.direction_note: Direction identifies the specified mechanism; it does not assert one-way influence across the entire relationship.

segments.text: Held 2026 reporting describes Kirkland’s May partnership with Legora alongside investment in a custom AI platform and other third-party tools.

Analyst inference: Legora gains a named large-firm deployment relationship; Kirkland obtains outside capability while retaining its internal-build programme. The combination may give Kirkland options and Legora a route into substantial workflows.
The reporting does not disclose deal size, exclusivity, scope of deployment or performance. The firm’s internal investment is not evidence it will replace Legora.
Named deployed workflows and integration details would clarify how strategic the partnership becomes.

P-19.direction_note: Direction identifies the specified mechanism; it does not assert one-way influence across the entire relationship.

segments.text: A&O Shearman’s 2025 announcement describes agents developed with Harvey for complex legal tasks, intended for internal rollout and sale to clients and other law firms.

Analyst inference: A&O Shearman contributes legal expertise and Harvey contributes its application platform to agents intended for internal and external use. Distribution to clients and other firms could turn legal know-how into products used beyond the firm’s own engagements.
The firm announcement supports joint development and proposed sale, not actual customer adoption, intellectual-property allocation or a realised revenue stream.
External purchasers, contractual rights and sustained product use would show whether the collaboration becomes a durable product business.

P-20.direction_note: Direction identifies the specified mechanism; it does not assert one-way influence across the entire relationship.

segments.text: The held firm announcement says ContractMatrix was built for in-house counsel through collaboration with Harvey and Microsoft.

Analyst inference: The collaboration combines legal expertise, an application partner and Microsoft’s participation in a contract tool. It illustrates a firm co-producing a tool for in-house users rather than remaining only a technology purchaser.

The passage establishes participation in ContractMatrix but does not specify Microsoft’s technical contribution, ownership, exclusivity or revenues. Those must not be inferred from its other legal products.
Technical and commercial detail plus evidence of in-house adoption would determine the strength of this relationship.

P-21.direction_note: Direction identifies the specified mechanism; it does not assert one-way influence across the entire relationship.

segments.text: Ford’s general counsel says the company expects to expand relationships with innovators and curtail reliance on laggards while investing in in-house AI and paying for demonstrable gains.

Analyst inference: A named buyer signals that future work can favour providers that deliver demonstrable gains. Continued internal investment supplies a possible alternative to outside work and makes provider responsiveness relevant to allocation.
This is Ford’s general counsel’s intention, not an observed termination or a claim against every large firm. No specific retained firm is identified in the cited passages.
Actual matter reallocations, fee arrangements and named provider changes would distinguish implementation from a bargaining signal.

P-22.direction_note: Direction identifies the specified mechanism; it does not assert one-way influence across the entire relationship.

segments.text: Commentary identifies Crosby as building on Claude; Anthea Roberts and David B. Wilkins list Crosby among Claude for Legal’s launch users. Embedded reporting describes Crosby taking responsibility for the legal work.

Analyst inference: Crosby can build its negotiation service on external model capability while retaining responsibility for delivering the legal work. The supplier provides technical capability; Crosby still has to add workflow and service value.

The stack account is commentary and Roberts–Wilkins’ launch-user account. Neither establishes exclusive dependence, contract terms or a finding that Anthropic performs Crosby’s lawyer responsibilities.
Verified changes in architecture, model substitution and delivery quality would change the assessment.

P-23.direction_note: Direction identifies the specified mechanism; it does not assert one-way influence across the entire relationship.

segments.text: Crosby’s founder describes conducting contract negotiations end to end and says one customer pays per contract rather than expanding its internal legal team.

Analyst inference: An end-to-end contract service gives an in-house team a potential alternative to adding headcount for certain work. Per-contract purchasing can turn a fixed staffing decision into a variable service expense, while the provider accepts responsibility for delivery.
The cost and headcount account comes from Crosby’s founder in an auto-captioned interview. It is one customer example, not proof of savings across buyers or a supplier relationship with Ford.
Independent client evidence on quality, cost and repeat use would strengthen the reading; substantial unpriced buyer-side supervision would narrow it.

P-24.direction_note: Direction identifies the specified mechanism; it does not assert one-way influence across the entire relationship.

segments.text: Sacra’s held account says Harvey customers can route tasks to Anthropic and Google models alongside existing OpenAI systems.

Analyst inference: OpenAI provides one of the model options behind Harvey’s workflows. Harvey combines that capability with its own application and implementation layer; multi-model routing gives Harvey some flexibility in allocating tasks.
The evidence does not disclose OpenAI traffic share, exclusivity or price. The OpenAI Startup Fund’s investment is a separate tie and is not imported as an OpenAI holding.
Model-routing changes, contractual terms and the costs of replacing OpenAI for specific workflows would establish how much leverage this input provides.

P-25.direction_note: Direction identifies the specified mechanism; it does not assert one-way influence across the entire relationship.

segments.text: Trade commentary discusses OpenAI’s legal-product plans, Roberts–Wilkins describe its legal vertical, and Harvey’s CEO says he expects long-term competition with model companies. This supports a hypothesis of rivalry, not an observed bilateral outcome.

Analyst inference: Supplying models while developing legal applications can put OpenAI in competition for tasks currently mediated by Harvey. Direct access to model capability is an advantage only if the application and implementation meet users’ needs.

The pair-specific rivalry remains inference. The sources describe OpenAI’s legal entry and Harvey’s CEO’s general expectation of competition with model companies; they do not identify a lost procurement or customer migration between these two.
Documented head-to-head purchasing or switching would strengthen the claim; continued complementary use through Harvey would constrain it.

actor_depth.research_basis: Held corpus plus targeted retrieval from Second Chair MCP. Source publication dates and captured versions govern claims; general analytical mechanisms are explicitly labelled.
actor_depth.selection_rationale: Twelve named actors test the platform–firm–buyer chain, contrasting build, buy, partnership and direct service provision. Four group readings retain the buyer, large-firm, insurer and junior-workforce perspectives that a co-mention diagram alone can obscure. Selection is provisional and does not infer power from graph size.

power.text: California's guidance says AI must not diminish professional judgment, the lawyer remains fully responsible for outputs, and the more autonomy an AI system has, the more supervisory controls matter. One aggregator analysis reports that professional liability carriers increasingly expect renewal documentation mapped to ABA Formal Opinion 512. The ABA President signed the G7 Bars Statement on AI with representatives of all G7 bars in March 2024. According to Younger, a practitioner who supports the resolution, the ABA House of Delegates overwhelmingly passed Resolution 402 in August 2022, reaffirming its steadfast opposition to nonlawyer ownership.

sections.heading: Conditional permission
sections.text: Formal Opinion 512 enumerates the duties lawyers using generative AI must consider; the Year 2 report records the state ethics opinions that followed; the task force warns of stratification between organisations that can afford enterprise-grade systems and those that cannot, and its judicial guidelines hold that AI may assist but never replace judicial judgment.

A Legal Cheek item, linking to its November 2025 report, says BPP, ULaw, Oxford and King's College London struck a deal with Harvey, embedding its tools and teaching materials into their law courses. power.text: Microsoft announced the Legal Agent on its Copilot blog on 30 April 2026, describing it as analysing the full agreement, drilling into clauses and comparing versions to spot risks and obligations. In Anthea Roberts and David B. Harvey plans a Microsoft 365 Copilot integration that lets lawyers invoke Harvey inside Copilot, and Thomson Reuters says CoCounsel Legal will connect to Microsoft 365. Legal Cheek reports that Shoosmiths' AI-usage bonus initiative is backed by a partnership with Microsoft. Thomson Reuters.description: The most-windowed publisher: acquirer of Casetext, victor over ROSS on headnote copying, and the incumbent whose CTO says the control point is defensible output, not where work starts
limitations: Corporate releases are self-descriptions; the litigation record is a district-court summary judgment under appeal per the retained commentary.

power.text: A court record shows that when Ross, a competitor with an AI legal-research tool, asked to license Westlaw's content, Thomson Reuters refused. Ross later shut down, a press report says, because Thomson Reuters' lawsuit had crippled its ability to raise financing. The case, Thomson Reuters v. ROSS, was argued at the Third Circuit on 11 June 2026 and is the first appeal of a decision related to whether training an AI model on copyrighted works, here Westlaw headnotes, is fair use. Thomson Reuters rebuilt CoCounsel on Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK, a two-way integration. CoCounsel Legal is a Claude for Legal connector.

sections.heading: Buy, sue, rebuild
sections.text: Closed the Casetext purchase; framed ROSS's use of Westlaw headnotes as commercial copying to build a substitute and obtained summary judgment on actual copying; rebuilt CoCounsel Legal from the ground up and now describes it as working like a senior associate.

sections.heading: Convergence, not centre
sections.text: Hron's framing — a convergence of roles, the control point being accurate, grounded, defensible output — is the incumbent's answer to the substrate reading of Claude for Legal. The Geek in Review hosts treat the Anthropic–Thomson Reuters announcements as raising the question of what a model provider now is. The Stanford study, meanwhile, tested Westlaw's AI-assisted research and found hallucination persisting.

power.text: In a letter of 5 September 2024, the court decided that further narrowing the sandbox would better promote its objectives and align with its jurisdiction over the practice of law in Utah, adding a Utah nexus to the innovation requirement. limitations: Affiliation and bibliography co-mentions dominate.

sections.heading: Evaluation and policy
sections.text: Stanford's RegLab tested the research tools; Suffolk's Perlman catalogued law-school AI policies and Berkeley's restrictive one drew attention; the ABA task force records Suffolk's and Stanford's teaching tools; IAALS's Utah reading is recorded dissent. Harvard's Center on the Legal Profession is the home of the Big Four and in-house scholarship and of the Roberts–Wilkins essay series on AI and the legal profession.

academy.summary: Harvard, Stanford and its labs, Suffolk, Berkeley, Georgetown, NYU, Michigan, Vanderbilt, Yale, Columbia, MIT, the NBER, the ACM, IEEE, ACL, RAND, IAALS, the American Bar Foundation, NALP and University of Minnesota Law clear the floor (calculated). The passages are studies, reports and law-school AI policies.
academy.title: Academy & research

ai-native-firm.headline: A small class with the densest capital ties: firms that combine software, employed lawyers and venture or private-equity money
limitations: Class synthesis of six actors; vendor and investor statements are self-interested.

sections.heading: The model and its money
sections.text: Crosby employs lawyers and engineers, owns liability and is backed by Sequoia and others; Norm Law exists for Bain Capital's deals; Garfield.Law was authorised by the SRA and won a county-court case without a lawyer on the pre-trial work; Eudia's Arizona firm was newsworthy enough to headline a podcast. The IBA piece states what they reject: leverage.

sections.heading: The counter-example
sections.text: Atrium raised heavily, promised to revolutionise legal services and shut down after failing to deliver better efficiency than a traditional firm — the corpus's reminder that the model has failed before.

ai-native-firm.summary: Six providers clear the floor (calculated) and the class has the strongest class-level association with capital by calculated NPMI. Crosby, Norm Ai, Eudia, Covenant, Garfield AI and Atrium are the members; the passages record their funding, their regulatory openings and, in Atrium's case, failure.
ai-native-firm.title: AI-native legal provider

alsp.headline: Three providers whose co-mentions come from the scholarship that named them alternatives and the Big Four that absorbed the category
limitations: Class of three; Consilio has no retrieved passage in this run.

sections.heading: Blurring into the mainstream
sections.text: Axiom presents itself as an alternative while promising the professional development and peer network of a traditional firm; UnitedLex's ULX venture claimed to fix what outsourcing and hybrid staffing had failed to fix; Axiom's own release is a satisfaction-and-cost claim. Consolidation with the Big Four and law-firm-owned captives is the scholarship's theme.

alsp.summary: Axiom, UnitedLex and Consilio clear the floor (calculated). The class's strongest association is with the Big Four, and the passages are the Wilkins studies on taking the 'alternative' out of alternative providers.
alsp.title: ALSP / flexible resourcing

analyst-press.headline: Twenty-nine outlets, consultancies and podcasts; the class’s strongest association is with named individuals because it is where they are introduced, quoted and cited
limitations: Press co-mention records coverage, not commercial or institutional ties.

sections.heading: Venue, not relationship
sections.text: Court footnotes cite the New York Times and Reuters; a podcast introduces its hosts and guests; Ambrogi reports on Thomson Reuters, Perlman's archive and ILTACON; Abramowitz records that Harvey draws the most clicks. McKinsey and the consultancies are also subjects (internal bots) and, in Goldman's case, authors of exposure estimates. The class's position in the network is a measure of who the corpus reads about through them.

analyst-press.summary: Artificial Lawyer, LawSites, Legally Disrupted, Technically Legal, The Geek in Review, Legaltech Hub, Law.com, Law360, Legal IT Insider, the FT, NYT, WSJ, Guardian, CNN, CNBC, TechCrunch, Forbes, HBR, McKinsey, BCG, Gartner and others. Their co-mentions are venue effects: they publish, cite and host the actors.
analyst-press.title: Analyst, consultancy & press

big-four.headline: Four firms always named together: a class whose within-class density is complete by calculation because the scholarship treats them as one competitor
limitations: Complete within-class density reflects list mentions, not coordination.

sections.heading: Named as a bloc
sections.text: The Wilkins studies list the four together at every step — the Big Five push into law, ABS licences, integration of affiliated firms — and the press names them together for their internal AI assistants; Google lists Deloitte and KPMG as Gemini Enterprise for Legal partners. KPMG Law US's Arizona approval and Wilkins's comment that it extends a tech-enabled multidisciplinary model are the member-level passages.

big-four.summary: Deloitte, EY, KPMG and PwC are named together in the Big Four studies, in the consulting-bot press and in Google's partner list; KPMG's Arizona licence is the one member-specific event.
big-four.title: Big Four

capital.headline: Investors are named at funding events; the class’s strongest ties are to the AI-native firms and vendors it prices, and its members split across two communities
limitations: Investor statements are self-interested; valuations are prices, not use.

sections.heading: Pricing the platform layer
sections.text: The recorded rounds put Sequoia, Kleiner Perkins, Coatue and Andreessen Horowitz behind Harvey, Accel, General Catalyst, Bain Capital and Y Combinator behind Legora, and Sequoia, Cooley and Elad Gil behind Crosby. Harvey's own partnership with the LegalTech Fund to invest in startups makes a vendor an investor.

sections.heading: Private equity as client and owner
sections.text: Bain Capital is both investor in and client of Norm Law; Blackstone funds Clio's debt and joined Anthropic's services venture aimed at consulting; Kirkland's private-equity identity is the reason its AI investment is read as strategic.

capital.summary: Twelve investors clear the floor (calculated). Sequoia, Kleiner Perkins, Coatue, Andreessen Horowitz, Elad Gil, the OpenAI Startup Fund and the LegalTech Fund sit with Harvey and the labs; General Catalyst and Y Combinator with Legora; Bain Capital, Blackstone and Goldman Sachs with the AI-native firms and elite-firm cluster.
capital.title: Capital (VC/PE)

client-inhouse.headline: The class the network under-represents: thirteen actors, sparse ties, while the passages record buyers insourcing and setting the terms
limitations: Sparse class by calculation; survey figures describe respondents, not the market.
'Legal Aid Society' resolved to the Legal Aid Society of Riverside in one passage.

sections.heading: Buyers act more than they are named
sections.text: Ford's general counsel tells firms the company is outpacing their AI adoption and will curtail reliance on laggards; the curator essay collects survey figures on insourcing and reduced reliance on outside counsel; Harbor records falling outside-counsel spend expectations; the ACC/Everlaw survey records adoption more than doubling; Microsoft cut in-house counsel in a move read as AI-related. None of these buyers is a high-degree node.

sections.heading: Why the class is sparse
sections.text: The corporates in this class are named as Legora's or Harvey's investors and customers (Salesforce Ventures, Barclays) or as capital-expenditure comparators (Amazon, Apple), and General Electric appears as the historical exemplar of the in-house counsel movement. The corpus writes about buyers through vendors and scholars, not in their own voice, which the network faithfully reproduces.

client-inhouse.summary: The ACC, CLOC, Ford, General Electric, Cisco, Salesforce, Amazon, Apple, Walmart, Barclays, Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan and Nvidia clear the floor (calculated) but the class has low within-density and its corporate members are mostly named as investors, employers or comparators rather than as legal buyers.
client-inhouse.title: Client / in-house legal

foundation-model.headline: The class with the most windows by calculation, named as substrate beneath others’ products and, since the legal launches, as a competitor
limitations: Class synthesis; the labs compete with one another.

sections.heading: Substrate
sections.text: CoCounsel was built on OpenAI's model, LexisNexis announced an OpenAI collaboration and a multi-model approach, GPT-4 passed the bar exam in the Katz study, and Harvey began with GPT-3. These passages name a lab as an input, which is why the class is everywhere and specifically connected to no one.

sections.heading: Competitor
sections.text: Claude for Legal placed Anthropic at the heart of the market with the vendors as participants; Microsoft shipped a Legal Agent in Word; OpenAI hired Ironclad's founder for a legal vertical; Google launched Gemini Enterprise for Legal with a partner network. Artificial Lawyer counts three giants and asks where lawyers live; the antimonopoly article notes that providers dependent on one another's models have private incentives not to sue.

foundation-model.summary: OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, Google, Meta AI, Mistral, DeepSeek, xAI, Perplexity and IBM clear the floor (calculated). OpenAI alone has the largest window count of any actor, yet lower degree than the vendors — its mentions are spread across the products and studies built on its models.
foundation-model.title: Foundation model lab

incumbent-firm.headline: Buyers, builders and brands: the firms are named as vendor customers, as proprietary builders and as the source of talent for their challengers
limitations: Class synthesis; members compete and do not share a position.
Announcements state strategy, not outcomes.

sections.heading: Customers first
sections.text: The firm passages are overwhelmingly partnership announcements: A&O's exclusive Harvey launch and agentic agents, Linklaters' firmwide Legora roll-out, Cleary's strategic partnership, Ashurst and others deploying Harvey agents. Harvey's own claim that over half the Am Law 100 use it is a vendor figure.

sections.heading: Building rather than buying
sections.text: Kirkland's decision to build its own platform with Legora, Clifford Chance's Assist on the Microsoft Azure OpenAI platform, Cleary's acquisition of a generative-AI developer and the Australian firms trialling Copilot show a build-or-configure strand; the FT's account has Kirkland paying for it out of profits otherwise shared among equity partners. Whether the tournament-and-leverage model that funds these firms survives is the class's open question.

incumbent-firm.summary: Thirty-one firms clear the document floor (calculated). Their co-mentions are dominated by vendor partnership announcements — A&O and Harvey, Linklaters and Cleary with Legora — with a second layer of proprietary building (Kirkland's platform, Clifford Chance Assist on Azure OpenAI) and a third in which their lawyers staff AI-native firms.
incumbent-firm.title: Incumbent law firm

incumbent-publisher.headline: The most densely interconnected class by calculation, and the one whose passages are about owning and defending content
limitations: Class synthesis; Bloomberg Law is here as a publisher and a venue.

sections.heading: Data as the defended asset
sections.text: Thomson Reuters bought Casetext and won on copying of Westlaw headnotes against ROSS; LexisNexis supplies primary law and citations into Harvey while RELX invests; Wolters Kluwer's Smartlaw survived a German challenge to automated document services. The CTO's claim that the control point is defensible output is the class position.

incumbent-publisher.summary: Thomson Reuters, LexisNexis, RELX, Wolters Kluwer, vLex and Bloomberg Law clear the floor (calculated); the class's within-density is among the highest. Their passages are acquisitions, alliances, litigation over headnotes and the multi-model sourcing that lets them supply everyone.
incumbent-publisher.title: Legal information incumbent

individual.headline: Sixty-two people: founders, hosts, judges, scholars; their strongest ties are to their own institutions and co-authors, which the calculator withholds from drawing
limitations: Individuals below the profiling threshold have mention-level or gap profiles.

sections.heading: Who the individuals are
sections.text: Founders (Weinberg, Pereyra, Junestrand, Boehmig), hosts and commentators (Lambert, Gebauer, Ambrogi, Abramowitz, Tromans, Shaver, Main, Martin, Leonard), leaders of institutions (McCormack, John Roberts, Anthea Roberts, Wakeling, Walters), and scholars (Wilkins, Galanter, Henderson, Susskind, Hadfield, Rhode, Sandefur, Ho and the Stanford authors, Choi and Schwarcz, the economists). Their co-mentions come from podcast introductions, bylines and author lists, and the passages cited in their profiles say what each actually claims.

individual.summary: The largest class by calculation. Person–institution pairs (Abramowitz–Legally Disrupted, Main–Technically Legal, Shaver–Legaltech Hub, Martin–LawDroid, Ambrogi–LawSites, Boehmig–Ironclad) are the strongest associations in the network and are flagged as affiliations; the strongest drawn pairs are co-hosts and co-authors.
individual.title: Named individual

actor_ids: Law Society of England and Wales
Supreme Court of the United States
regulator-court.headline: Thirty-three institutions named for what they permit, prohibit and sanction; the class anchors the largest community
limitations: Class synthesis across jurisdictions; regimes are not transferable.

sections.heading: Permission and prohibition
sections.text: The SRA authorised an AI-only firm; Arizona licensed KPMG; Utah narrowed its sandbox; the California bar investigated DoNotPay; the ABA issued Formal Opinion 512 and the NYC Bar chose guardrails over new rules; the Bar Council told barristers that reliable tools are not improper if properly understood; the EU AI Act entered into force and is now being reopened.

sections.heading: Sanction
sections.text: Mata v. Avianca states the gatekeeping duty; the Fifth and Sixth Circuits sanctioned fabricated citations and invoked inherent authority; Charlotin's database counts hundreds of such decisions; the Chief Justice's year-end report and the AO's letter to the Senate record the federal judiciary's own engagement. The Supreme Court's high brokerage partly reflects reporter citations in these opinions.

regulator-court.summary: US and non-US regulators, bars, courts and international bodies are named together in ethics opinions, sanctions orders, sandbox rules and guidance. Their co-mentions are legal-document co-citation as much as institutional interaction.
regulator-court.title: Regulator, bar or court

vendor-legal-ai.headline: The class that generates the network: vendors are named with firms as customers, with publishers as partners or rivals, and with labs as substrate
limitations: Class synthesis; members compete.
Vendor claims are self-descriptions.

sections.heading: Named with everyone
sections.text: Harvey is named with A&O, LexisNexis, Microsoft, Google and Anthropic; Legora with Linklaters, Cleary, Kirkland and its investors; Casetext with Thomson Reuters and OpenAI; Clio with vLex. The Claude for Legal launch named four of them at once, and Ambrogi reads the vendors' response as integrating deeply rather than fleeing.

sections.heading: The evaluators’ counter-view
sections.text: The same vendors are named by the empirical studies that tested them, and the recorded finding is that hallucination persists and hallucination-free claims are ungrounded.

vendor-legal-ai.summary: Twenty-eight vendors clear the floor (calculated) and the class holds the two highest-degree nodes (Harvey, Legora). Its co-mentions with incumbent publishers and firms are the densest cross-class ties in the network by calculated support.
vendor-legal-ai.title: Legal-AI vendor

community:0.disclosure: This is a statistical co-mention community, not a coalition or evidence of shared intent.
community:0.headline: A community where the Big Four’s long march into law, the A&O–Harvey partnership and the ALSP literature are written about together
limitations: Computed community, not a coalition; the firms named here compete with the Big Four they are grouped with.
Firm and vendor announcements are self-descriptions.

sections.heading: The A&O–Harvey spine
sections.text: A&O Shearman is the firm the corpus names first for Harvey: the exclusive launch partnership put the platform in front of thousands of lawyers, ContractMatrix was built with Harvey and Microsoft, and the agentic agents were designed to be sold to clients and other firms as well as used internally. Wakeling's own framing is that the firm has put its lawyers' judgment into the tech stack alongside the vendor's model. These are firm and vendor announcements; they state strategy, not verified outcomes.

sections.heading: The Big Four as a recurring competitor
sections.text: Deloitte, EY, KPMG and PwC co-occur here because the Wilkins–Esteban–Ferrer studies trace their re-entry into legal services: ABS licences in England and Wales, integration of affiliated law firms into the networks, and the more-for-less climate that makes them formidable competitors. KPMG's Arizona licence, recorded elsewhere, is the current chapter of the same story.

sections.heading: ALSPs blur the boundary
sections.text: Axiom and UnitedLex enter through the same scholarship: Axiom presenting itself as an alternative while reassuring lawyers and clients it has the features of a traditional firm without the costs, UnitedLex's ULX venture claiming to be the most disruptive change since lawyers began billing time. Axiom's own release is a vendor claim about client satisfaction and cost, not independent evidence.

sections.heading: Why the press and the law schools are here
sections.text: Harvard Law School, Columbia and Yale, the Financial Times, Forbes and Reuters are members because the same studies and firm stories cite them or are published by them. The Financial Times' Kirkland story and Reuters' Casetext report are venue co-mentions; they place the outlets in the community without implying any relationship with the firms.

sections.heading: Roberts and Wilkins as co-authors
sections.text: Anthea Roberts enters the recalculated community beside David B. Wilkins and Harvard Law School. The series introduction names them together as authors, recording their substantive collaboration on the project.

community:0.summary: This grouping joins A&O Shearman and its AI lead David Wakeling, the Big Four and their ALSP cousins (Axiom, UnitedLex), several Am Law and City firms, three law schools and the business press. The passages behind it are of two kinds: firm announcements of AI partnerships, and the Harvard Center on the Legal Profession's scholarship on the Big Four and alternative providers. It is a market circuit with a strong academic-citation spine.
community:0.title: Global firms, the Big Four, ALSPs and the elite press

community:1.disclosure: This is a statistical co-mention community, not a coalition or evidence of shared intent.
community:1.headline: The funding-and-model-supply nexus: labs that are suppliers, partners and rivals, and the investors who priced Harvey into the platform layer
limitations: Computed community, not a coalition; the labs compete with the vendors they fund and supply.
Valuations and customer counts are vendor or investor figures.

sections.heading: Capital priced the platform
sections.text: The rounds are reported in sequence — Series B with Elad Gil and Kleiner Perkins, Series C led by Google Ventures, Series D led by Sequoia, Series E led by Kleiner Perkins and Coatue — then the Andreessen Horowitz-led round and the growth round co-led by GIC and Sequoia that took the company past a billion dollars raised. Sequoia's co-leading of three rounds is itself reported as unusual. These are reported events; valuations are investor prices, not measures of use.

sections.heading: Labs as supplier, partner and rival
sections.text: Harvey was built on GPT-3 and its founders came from Meta and Google research; the OpenAI Startup Fund invested; and by the time of the Claude for Legal launch Harvey was describing a deepened partnership with Anthropic while the press asked whether Claude would take Harvey's and Legora's lunch. OpenAI's hiring of Ironclad's founder to lead a legal vertical is the clearest recorded move from supplier to competitor, and Artificial Lawyer counts three giants now launching legal-specific offerings.

sections.heading: The distribution question
sections.text: The lab-versus-vendor tension is about where lawyers 'live': Microsoft's Legal Agent inside Word, Claude for Word, Harvey inside Microsoft 365 Copilot and Harvey inside Gemini Enterprise are all bids for the same surface. Artificial Lawyer's counterpoint is that a firm going all-in with one lab limits its model choices, which is the vendors' argument for remaining model-agnostic.

sections.heading: Why the corporates are here
sections.text: Salesforce enters through Salesforce Ventures in Legora's round; Amazon, Apple, Meta and Microsoft are named together for their capital expenditure; Perplexity for crossing a valuation mark alongside OpenAI and Anthropic. None of these co-mentions records a legal-buyer relationship.

community:1.summary: OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft, Google and Meta AI sit with Sequoia, Kleiner Perkins, Coatue, Andreessen Horowitz, Elad Gil and the OpenAI Startup Fund, and with Harvey and its founders. The passages are funding announcements, lab launches into legal, and press that frames the labs as both the substrate and the threat. Salesforce, Amazon, Apple, Walmart and Nvidia appear as investors or as comparators, not as legal buyers.
community:1.title: Foundation labs, growth capital and Harvey

community:2.disclosure: This is a statistical co-mention community, not a coalition or evidence of shared intent.
community:2.headline: Where the corpus stages the organising question: the tournament-and-leverage model against firms that combine product, lawyers and outside capital
limitations: Computed community, not a coalition; the capital providers here fund the firms’ competitors.
Klover profiles are analyst reports, not audited figures.

sections.heading: The incumbents’ war chest and the build decision
sections.text: The Klover profile reads Kirkland's scale as the capacity to absorb enterprise AI costs across thousands of attorneys and to treat technology as strategic investment; the press then reports Kirkland partnering with Legora to build a custom platform rather than rely on third-party tools, paid out of revenues that would otherwise be shared among equity partners. The curator essay's paradox — rates rising on captive bet-the-company work while general counsel move moderately complex work downstream — is the demand-side context.

sections.heading: AI-native firms as the counter-model
sections.text: Crosby is described from inside as a neofirm: lawyers from Kirkland and Wachtell, engineers from Ramp and Stripe, liability owned, work taken end to end, venture money from Sequoia and others; Cooley's investment in a rival firm is reported as notable in itself. Norm Law was created for its investor's own deals; Y Combinator's request for startups told founders to start a law firm staffed with agents rather than sell software to incumbents. The IBA article names the mechanism these firms reject: leverage, the margin between associate salaries and billing rates.

sections.heading: Why the tournament scholars are here
sections.text: Galanter and Henderson's elastic tournament and Wilkins's account of Heineman at General Electric are in this community because the same passages that discuss elite-firm economics cite them; the tournament is the institution whose viability the AI-native model tests. A cautionary member is Atrium, the earlier hybrid that shut down after failing to beat a traditional firm's efficiency.

community:2.summary: Kirkland & Ellis, Cravath, Davis Polk, Sullivan & Cromwell, Wachtell, Cooley and Sidley sit with Crosby, Eudia, Norm Ai and Covenant, with Bain Capital, Blackstone, Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan and Vanguard, with Law.com and Bloomberg Law, and with Galanter and Henderson. The passages are about firm economics and about the new providers financed to bypass them.
community:2.title: Elite transactional firms, AI-native providers and private capital

actor_ids: Law Society of England and Wales
Supreme Court of the United States
community:3.disclosure: This is a statistical co-mention community, not a coalition or evidence of shared intent.
community:3.headline: The largest community by calculation is held together by permission and prohibition, and by the scholars and reformers who argue over both
limitations: Computed community, not a coalition; it contains regulators, the providers they investigate and the scholars who criticise both.
Jurisdiction-specific regimes (UPL, ABS, SRA) are not transferable.

sections.heading: Permission: sandboxes, ABS licences and an AI-only firm
sections.text: The SRA authorised Garfield.Law as the first purely AI-based firm while keeping named solicitors accountable for every output; Utah's sandbox was narrowed to entities serving underserved consumers and its participant count fell; Arizona licensed KPMG Law US as an ABS. The IAALS reading of Utah's early data as refuting fears of harm is a recorded Opposes stance against the majority view on ownership reform, and the KPMG commentary is another.

sections.heading: Prohibition: UPL, sanctions and the courts
sections.text: The California bar's investigation of DoNotPay is recorded in the FTC's complaint; Upsolve's challenge to New York's UPL statute is recorded both in the Second Circuit's opinion and in testimony calling the rules exclusion rather than protection; the courts' gatekeeping role is stated in Mata v. Avianca and extended by the Fifth and Sixth Circuits' sanctions opinions. The Chief Justice's year-end report is the passage that puts the Supreme Court into this community.

sections.heading: Access to justice: funders and designers
sections.text: The LSC's technology summit report asks the corporation to lead responsible AI innovation across the field and to help grantees cut through hype; the NYSBA committee argues legal aid should embrace AI because it meets less than a tenth of need. Hagan's call for statewide AI stewards is the design-side counterpart. The court-administration paper's warning that AI tools may widen the knowledge imbalance between self-represented litigants and represented clients is the recorded counter-view.

sections.heading: Why McCormack, Leonard and Susskind are here
sections.text: Bridget McCormack and Jen Leonard co-host a podcast and are one of the strongest drawable pairs by calculated NPMI; their episodes name the AAA, the Michigan Supreme Court and the regulators they discuss, which pulls them into this community. Susskind enters as the profession's best-known advocate of technological transformation, cited in the same access-to-justice and regulatory scholarship.

community:3.summary: Supreme courts, bars, the SRA, the Law Society, the Legal Services Board, the LSC, the FTC and the EU institutions are named together with DoNotPay, Upsolve, Garfield AI and LawDroid, and with Susskind, Furlong, Hadfield, Rhode, Sandefur, McCormack and Leonard. The passages are ethics opinions, sanctions orders, sandbox rules, UPL enforcement and access-to-justice reports. It is where the corpus decides who may deliver AI-enabled help.
community:3.title: Regulators, courts, bars and access to justice

community:4.disclosure: This is a statistical co-mention community, not a coalition or evidence of shared intent.
community:4.headline: A podcast circuit: the strongest pair in the whole drawn network is two co-hosts, and the community is their guests and venues
limitations: Computed community produced largely by transcript boilerplate; do not read it as a professional network.

sections.heading: Why the edge is so strong
sections.text: Every episode opens with both hosts introducing the show and closes with the same thanks to listeners; the hosts are therefore named together in every transcript window, which is why Lambert–Gebauer is the strongest drawable association by calculated NPMI. The content in between is substantive — for example the hosts framing whether Anthropic is still just a model provider after its Thomson Reuters connector — but the association itself is structural.

sections.heading: The guests who join the community
sections.text: Ed Walters is introduced as vLex's chief strategy officer and discusses the AI Smackdown in which Vincent AI was compared with Lexis+ and Westlaw; Nikki Shaver appears as Legaltech Hub's co-founder and argues that trusted judgment, not lawyer time, is becoming the scarce asset. ILTA enters through Ambrogi's report of record ILTACON attendance.

community:4.summary: Greg Lambert and Marlene Gebauer, Ed Walters of vLex, Nikki Shaver of Legaltech Hub, Stephanie Wilkins, ILTA and vLex form a small community whose edges are produced by episode intros and outros. It is the clearest case in the network of co-mention measuring who speaks together rather than who works together.
community:4.title: The Geek in Review circuit

community:5.disclosure: This is a statistical co-mention community, not a coalition or evidence of shared intent.
community:5.headline: A citation cluster whose co-mentions with vendors come from testing their products and whose internal edges are co-authorship
limitations: Computed community; author-list and bibliography co-mention dominate its internal edges.
Studies report findings for the tools and periods tested; they are not current product assessments.

sections.heading: Evaluation, not partnership
sections.text: The Magesh–Surani–Dahl–Suzgun–Ho study co-mentions LexisNexis and Thomson Reuters because it tested Lexis+ AI and Westlaw's AI-assisted research and found the hallucination problem persisting despite retrieval augmentation; it records the vendors' hallucination-free claims as true only in the narrowest sense and calls for hard evidence before such claims are treated as grounded. The Choi–Monahan–Schwarcz trial is the other spine: the first randomised controlled trial of AI assistance in legal analysis.

sections.heading: The economists and the exposure estimates
sections.text: Acemoglu and Restrepo, Autor, Brynjolfsson and their co-authors co-occur through reference lists and through the task-based framework Acemoglu uses to argue that generative AI's larger gains require reorienting the industry away from general conversational tools. Goldman Sachs' exposure estimate and McKinsey's internal bots put the consultancies in the same neighbourhood; Mollick's cybernetic-teammate experiment is the field-experiment counterpart.

sections.heading: Links to access-to-justice research
sections.text: Hagan's Legal Design Lab, Stanford's law-school labs and the National Center for State Courts now sit in the regulator and access-to-justice community after recalculation. Their work remains cited across this research circuit; the displayed partition is a co-mention result, not a fixed institutional classification.

community:5.summary: The Stanford hallucination study's authors, the Minnesota randomised-trial authors, the labour economists (Brynjolfsson, Autor, Acemoglu, Restrepo, Rock, Manning), Mollick, Katz, Surden, the NBER, MIT, Stanford's Digital Economy Lab, McKinsey, RAND, the ACM and IEEE, and elite press form the empirical and economic research circuit. Its strongest edges are author lists; its links to the market are evaluations.
community:5.title: The empirical and economic research circuit

community:6.disclosure: This is a statistical co-mention community, not a coalition or evidence of shared intent.
community:6.headline: Legora’s customer roster and investors, the firms that adopted it, and the commentators who narrate the Harvey–Legora rivalry
limitations: Computed community, not a coalition; the firms listed are Legora customers, not allies of one another.
Vendor growth figures are self-reported.

sections.heading: Customers and capital
sections.text: Legora reports scaling from a handful of adopters to more than a thousand firms and legal teams including White & Case, Linklaters and Barclays after a Y Combinator start; Linklaters and Cleary announced firmwide roll-outs, Cleary alongside its acquisition of a generative-AI product company; the Series D was led by Accel with General Catalyst, Y Combinator, Bain Capital and Salesforce Ventures among the investors, and the press then reported talks at a far higher valuation. Kirkland's proprietary build with Legora is the community's bridge to the elite-firm cluster.

sections.heading: The rivalry as recorded dissent
sections.text: Junestrand's recorded stances redirect and oppose the Harvey-centred narrative: it does not matter who was first but who is best; Legora is the platform where legal work happens; and the market is winner-takes-all with the leader taking almost everything. Thomson Reuters' CTO, in the vendor community, explicitly rejects any one company sitting at the centre. A law-firm voice in the same topic prefers bespoke builds to either platform.

sections.heading: Why the commentators are here
sections.text: Abramowitz's Legally Disrupted and Tromans's Artificial Lawyer generate co-mentions by design: the show introduces itself and its guests every episode, and Abramowitz records that nothing he writes draws more attention than Harvey. Their association with Legora is editorial coverage, not commercial relationship.

community:6.summary: Legora and Max Junestrand sit with Linklaters, Cleary Gottlieb, Latham, Skadden, Paul Weiss, White & Case, Dentons and Bird & Bird, with General Catalyst, Y Combinator and Barclays, and with Zach Abramowitz, Richard Tromans and Sandstone. The passages are Legora's own announcements, the firms' roll-outs, funding reports and the podcast that treats Harvey-versus-Legora as its recurring story.
community:6.title: Legora, the Magic Circle and Wall Street firms, growth capital and Legally Disrupted

community:7.disclosure: This is a statistical co-mention community, not a coalition or evidence of shared intent.
community:7.headline: Ownership, acquisition and litigation over data: the community where control of legal content is bought and defended
limitations: Computed community, not a coalition; several members are litigants or acquirer and target.
Vendor and publisher releases are self-descriptions.

sections.heading: Acquisition and litigation
sections.text: Thomson Reuters closed its purchase of Casetext, whose CoCounsel had coupled OpenAI's model with Casetext's own databases, and later rebuilt CoCounsel Legal from the ground up; it framed ROSS's use of Westlaw headnotes as commercial copying to build a substitute and won summary judgment on actual copying of thousands of headnotes. Clio's acquisition of vLex, with vLex's private-equity owner taking Clio stock, is the other recorded consolidation.

sections.heading: Alliances that cross the community boundary
sections.text: LexisNexis integrated its primary law, citator and AI into Harvey while RELX's venture arm invested in Harvey's rounds; LexisNexis also announced an OpenAI collaboration and describes a multi-model approach across AWS, Anthropic, Microsoft, Mistral and OpenAI. Thomson Reuters' CTO's account of Claude calling CoCounsel as a connected system is the incumbents' framing of where control now lies.

sections.heading: The consumer and contracts tier
sections.text: LegalZoom and Rocket Lawyer are the corpus's long-standing consumer platforms, with Kleiner Perkins and Google Ventures recorded as early backers; LegalZoom's North Carolina settlement produced a statutory UPL exemption for form-generating websites. Spellbook's investor describes targeting commercial contracts and in-house teams because law-firm software faces fee compression rather than market expansion.

community:7.summary: Thomson Reuters, LexisNexis, RELX, Wolters Kluwer, Casetext, ROSS, Clio, Ironclad, Spellbook, Relativity, Everlaw, iManage, NetDocuments, DocuSign, LegalZoom and Rocket Lawyer sit with Ambrogi's LawSites, Artificial Lawyer, Legal IT Insider, Luminance and Berkeley Law. The passages record acquisitions, alliances, a copyright judgment and the connector economy that followed Claude for Legal.

overview.built_from: The complete display retains 1,403 documents, 21,929 text windows, 268 actors, 14 classes, eight statistical communities and 1,647 backbone associations. Thirty-five interpreted relationships and 520 evidence records remain separate from the graph calculations.

L1_class|count.text: Each circle is an assigned actor category and size shows retained actor count. Lines are measured cross-category co-mentions; the layout supports reading and does not measure distance or agreement.
L1_class|count.title: Current view · categories

L2_entity|betweenness.text: Actor size shows betweenness in the complete co-mention backbone. Larger circles connect otherwise separated parts of this corpus conversation; this is not a measure of real-world brokerage or control.
L2_entity|betweenness.title: Current view · bridging

L2_entity|docs.text: Actor size shows document mentions in this corpus. Larger circles are more visible in the captured evidence base; they are not necessarily more powerful or influential.
L2_entity|docs.title: Current view · prevalence

L2_entity|eigenvector.text: Actor size shows connection to other well-connected actors in the main component. Faded circles lack this measure. Connectedness describes corpus position, not status or influence.
L2_entity|eigenvector.title: Current view · connectedness

findings.text: The graph joins names that share text windows more often than chance. Podcast outros, bibliographies, press venues and legal citations demonstrate why the line alone cannot establish a transaction, agreement, coalition or influence.
findings.title: An edge shows attention, not allegiance

findings.text: Harvey, LexisNexis, Thomson Reuters, Legora, Anthropic and Microsoft have the leading measured association and brokerage positions. The cited passages explain how model supply, content, capital, firm deployment and office software bring them into the same documents.
findings.title: The platform layer bridges otherwise distinct conversations

findings.text: The corpus places proprietary platforms inside incumbent firms beside product-plus-lawyers providers that own delivery and liability. The passages frame a contest over whether leverage remains load-bearing or gives way to a different production model.
findings.title: Two service models are competing to organise work

findings.text: Publishers, labs and legal platforms offer competing accounts of where defensible value sits: validated content, the foundation model, domain-specific deployment or a winning application layer. Their adjacency records the contest; it does not decide it.
findings.title: Control of client relationships and value capture remains contested

findings.text: Corporate legal departments are sparse, insurers do not clear the actor floor, and four retained actors sit at zero degree. The passages still record insourcing, spend pressure, insurance responses and in-house leadership; absence or isolation is a property of this corpus and threshold, not the world.
findings.title: The thresholded graph underrepresents consequential demand-side actors

findings.text: Winner-takes-all, convergence, ownership reform and bespoke-build positions appear among actors grouped by co-mention. Community membership therefore shows shared discursive context, never agreement, common intent or coalition.
findings.title: Disagreement sits inside statistical communities

overview.headline: The association network draws a map of the profession’s conversation; the platform layer bridges it, and the buyers and insurers who shape value capture are the actors it cannot see
overview.how_to_read: Start with the numbered findings, then select an actor. Major associations are sorted by measured lift and remain co-mention records. Passage-grounded interpreted relationships appear in a separate section with direction, kind, confidence and cited basis.

key.label: Circle
key.text: An actor, or an assigned actor category in Categories view.

key.label: Line
key.text: A measured co-mention association clearing the NPMI and shared-document floors.

key.label: Size
key.text: The selected corpus measure: prevalence, bridging or connectedness; actor count in Categories view.

key.label: Colour
key.text: Assigned actor category. Statistical communities are available in the reading and are not coalitions.

limitations: Corpus-bound reading of a calculated structure; neither the graph nor this interpretation measures market share or influence.
Retrieval is a targeted semantic sample; profiles marked source-limited or gap are disclosed as such rather than padded.
Counts quoted in prose are calculated from the sealed structure; figures, dates and money resolve to cited passages.
overview.summary: Read the eight statistical communities as neighbourhoods in the corpus conversation. The platform layer bridges several of them, while buyers, insurers and below-threshold actors expose what a co-mention map cannot establish on its own.
overview.verification: Every projection reference resolves to the accepted embedded contract. Actor, class, community, association, interpreted-relationship, evidence and source IDs are validated before this file is written.
overview.what_this_shows: This figure maps who is named together in the 1,403-document corpus. It supports readings about corpus visibility, association patterns and statistical communities. It does not measure market share, power, influence, agreement, transaction or coalition.

segments.text: Harvey is a legal AI platform vendor that says it partners with the majority of the Am Law 100 and over 500 in-house legal teams.

The analysis's reading: Harvey supports AI-enabled restructuring of legal work, matters greatly to how it unfolds and could shift stance if specific conditions change; it wants to keep its place in legal workflows as model providers move in.
It closed a $200 million round at an $11 billion valuation in March 2026 and was reported in August 2026 to be in talks at $15.5 billion.
Sacra reports that Harvey scrapped its earlier proprietary model after frontier models outperformed it, and that customers can route tasks to OpenAI, Anthropic and Google models.
LexisNexis places primary law and citations inside Harvey.
The analysis's reading: its position rests more on distribution, implementation staff and workflow lock-in than on a proprietary model.

The analysis's reading: speech and action align; the gap is verification, as customer and revenue figures are self-reported.

The analysis's reading: to mid-2027, Harvey closes a round above its March 2026 valuation. Would be wrong if no Harvey round is announced as closed between the August 2026 report and mid-2027, or one closes at or below $11 billion. In 2027, it buys a company aimed at in-house teams. Would be wrong if Harvey releases no custom foundation model for legal tasks by end-2029, or leaves the Claude for Legal connector list between January 2027 and end-2029.
Harvey contributed plugins to Claude for Legal's partner ecosystem.
Its CEO says he and his co-founder have said for years that long term they would end up competing with the model companies.
The analysis's reading: Harvey joins the ecosystems of the model providers it expects, in the long term, to compete with.

The analysis's reading: whether it can come to own a model layer is open.

segments.text: Thomson Reuters is a legal information incumbent whose CoCounsel Legal assistant is grounded in Westlaw and its other content.

The analysis's reading: it is mixed on AI-enabled restructuring of legal work, matters greatly to how it unfolds and is unlikely to shift stance; it wants its editorial content to stay the grounding layer that AI output cites, while distributing CoCounsel inside model providers' assistants.
A court record shows that when Ross, a competitor with an AI legal-research tool, asked to license Westlaw's content, Thomson Reuters refused.
Ross later shut down, a press report says, because Thomson Reuters' lawsuit had crippled its ability to raise financing.

The case, Thomson Reuters v. ROSS, was argued at the Third Circuit on 11 June 2026 and is the first appeal of a decision related to whether training an AI model on copyrighted works, here Westlaw headnotes, is fair use.
Thomson Reuters rebuilt CoCounsel on Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK, a two-way integration.
CoCounsel Legal is a Claude for Legal connector.

What that means is a contract is fundamentally just two humans negotiating on a handful of terms, but they're really collaborative and they're actually trying to get a deal closed, right? And so this is the price of the contract, how much money is being exchanged, and there's all these other small terms like limitations of liability or different warranties or assignments of IP, things that don't make a lot of sense, but there's a dollar value to each of those. And when you really understand that every contract, every transaction between two parties where there's a mutually beneficial exchange of value, where  dollars are being trading hands, there is going to be a contract that just makes that run. limitations_segments.text: Corpus snapshot contains 1501 curated published works, not a representative survey of lawyers or legal services. Source works and voice categories are not actors; actors are the entities the works talk about.

Counts of passages, customers, valuations or survey percentages describe the curated corpus and self-reported figures; they do not measure power, prevalence or market share. Vendor, investor and founder statements
are self-interested and are labelled as such.

Positions are coded relative to one axis — AI-enabled restructuring of legal production, pricing and staffing — not to every proposition in the corpus; a recorded topic stance is toward that topic's proposition, not toward this axis.
Every trajectory statement about 2029–2031 is an analyst estimate; observed source dates are retained as stated. Direction labels (rising/holding/declining) are judgments over bounded passages.

Retrieval is a ranked semantic sample: 49 retained requests, 8 rows per search_passages call. search_passages never returns the 124 restricted-distribution works; source_perspectives and topic_perspectives do return curator-extracted stances and verbatim quotes for restricted works (three cited passages
come from one), without serving their full passage text. Absence of an actor in these results is not proof of absence in all 1501 works.

Passages are bounded excerpts (search chunks and curator-extracted quotes); several are auto-captioned transcripts with garbled proper nouns. Claims support only what the quoted span carries; no external source was added and no accuracy verification against the world was performed.

Relationship typing follows the closed vocabulary of actors-data.schema.json; 'opposition' denotes competition or regulatory conflict stated in a passage, not hostility, and 'alliance' denotes a stated partnership, not agreement on the question.

The network is US-centred with UK, Canadian, Australian and Indian institutions; jurisdiction-bound regimes (UPL, ABS, SRA terms) are not transferable, and no global or Australian-only coverage is claimed.
Coalition membership reflects documented joint action; stability assessments (natural/opportunistic) are analyst classifications and the corpus does not measure coordination among members.
Junior-workforce and frontline evidence is anonymous and self-selected (RollOnFriday, Legal Cheek threads); it records sentiment, not measured employment outcomes.

Behavioural prediction is carried as analyst tiers (most likely / possible / unlikely but consequential / shift condition) inside the trajectory field of the eleven high-salience actors and as a stability class on every actor; no probabilities are assigned because the corpus supplies no base rates, and cascade effects between actors are stated only where a passage links them.

is an extraction-damaged curator quote whose subject survives only as a URL slug; it is cited with that damage disclosed and carries low confidence wherever used (Reform-state supreme courts and their oversight bodies; Direct-to-consumer legal AI and self-help providers; the relationship between them).

overview_sections.heading: Coalitions: what binds, splits and breaks them

segments.text: The analysis's reading: of thirteen candidate blocs, five show documented joint action among the profiled actors, meaning members act together through a shared instrument such as a launch, a signed statement or a jointly built framework; three of those bear on how AI restructures legal work, and none acts on how that work is priced or staffed.
In the Claude for Legal integration bloc, Thomson Reuters, LexisNexis, Harvey and Legora took part in the launch "in one way or another", a press account says,
CoCounsel Legal and Harvey ship as connectors,
and Harvey and Legora contributed plugins.
The analysis's reading: what binds it is exchange, as the model provider gains grounded content and firm workflows and vendors gain distribution inside the assistant lawyers use.
What splits it is rivalry: Harvey's CEO says he and his co-founder have said for years that long term they would end up competing with the model companies,
while Legora's CEO, on the prospect of model providers becoming competitors, says he isn't concerned; "the real value is in how they're applied," he wrote.
Trade press expects buyers to balance Claude for Legal against OpenAI's legal offering.
Commentary says vendors unable to say what they do beyond the practice-area plugin should expect an awkward few quarters.

The analysis's reading: the bloc would break if plugins came to match vendor workflows, or a participant made a rival model provider its primary supplier; members stay because inside is better than outside, not because they share a strategy.
The ABA President signed the G7 Bars Statement on AI with representatives of all G7 bars in March 2024,
stating an intent to cooperate on professional codes of conduct and underscoring a commitment to access to justice.
Permitted models differ in signatories' jurisdictions: the SRA authorised an AI-based firm with named solicitors accountable for its outputs,

while the task force of NYSBA, a voluntary bar association, says AI programs that do not involve a human lawyer in the loop in providing legal advice arguably violate the rules and may be considered unauthorised practice.
More than 100 buy-side legal and technology leaders across 82 organisations and law firms designed and validated Legal Benchmarks' shared AI evaluation framework in 2026,
and Harvey had released its own benchmark in 2024.
The analysis's reading: the other two real blocs are not legal-specific.
They are model-provider deployment ventures with private-equity partners, Anthropic's
and OpenAI's.

The analysis's reading: the blocs that bear on pricing, staffing and entry show parallel positions rather than documented joint action. Buyers press firms without coordinating, the reform pair has split, and the bar position against nonlawyer ownership could be bypassed without any rule change.
In September 2024 the Utah Supreme Court decided to narrow its sandbox further,
while Arizona licensed KPMG Law US in February 2025.
In the MSO structure law-firm counsel describe, a sponsor earns from the MSO's revenues under a long-term services agreement while the firm keeps professional judgment and client relationships.
Verification demands also run in parallel: one aggregator analysis reports carriers expecting renewal documentation mapped to ABA Formal Opinion 512,
and judges separately impose sanctions for filings with hallucinated citations.
The analysis's reading: no coordination is documented, and these parallel demands may constrain firms' AI use more than any declared bloc, though that comparison is not measured.
The corpus provider records 15 Opposes stances among 9,777 source stances in this curated corpus,
and states that 424 of the 9,777 push back in some form (redirect, oppose or mixed), and that positions measure stance toward each cluster's own framing, not absolute agreement.

The analysis's reading: opposition to AI-enabled restructuring is thin in recorded stances and shows no documented joint action on AI. Conduct that constrains how AI is used is substantial, in insurer conditions, court sanctions and bar duties, but it mainly targets unverified use; counting it as opposition to restructuring would overstate opposition. Resistance to restructuring itself is narrower: state bar UPL enforcement, equity partners' defensive rate posture and the bar position against nonlawyer ownership, whose one documented joint act is a 2022 ABA resolution that predates ChatGPT and does not address AI.
In State v. Coleman (Ohio Court of Appeals, 20 March 2026), listed in Damien Charlotin's tracker,
the court, sanctioning AI misuse, wrote that it does not condemn the use of AI in legal practice.

overview_sections.heading: Stakeholder reading of the whole field

segments.text: The analysis's reading: across the 32 actors read here, the contest over who gains AI's value in legal work runs on three fronts.
On the platform layer, model providers supply and partner with legal-AI vendors and publishers, as the Claude for Legal launch shows,
and Harvey's CEO says he and his co-founder have said for years that long term they would end up competing with the model companies.
On the buyer front, 61% of 657 in-house respondents to a 2025 ACC and Everlaw survey, co-published by a vendor, plan to push for change in how legal services are delivered and priced,
while the 2026 Thomson Reuters Institute and Georgetown Law Center report calls firm leaders' focus on rates defensive, not offensive.
The analysis's reading: on the public-facing front, enforcement bodies, reform courts, legal aid and consumer tools contest who may deliver AI help.
The analysis's reading: three 2024–2026 developments change that picture.

summary_segments.text: Twenty-seven subject actors are evidenced across the six agreed focus areas. The value-capture contest runs on three fronts: (1) a platform layer where foundation-model providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft) have become suppliers, partners and rivals to the venture-funded vendors (Harvey, Legora) and the data-holding publishers (Thomson Reuters, LexisNexis); (2) a buyer front where corporate legal departments insource, audit invoices and reward AI-fast counsel while large firms defend rate-led profits, mid-market firms split, and Big Four, ALSP and AI-native providers compete for process work; and (3) a public-facing front where UPL enforcement, reform-state courts, legal aid and consumer providers contest who may deliver AI help to the unrepresented. Professional judgment is gated by courts (sanctions and verification orders), bar ethics bodies (conditional permission), insurers (renewal conditions) and educators (divergent AI policies), while the junior workforce whose labour funded apprenticeship and partner profits is the constituency losing bargaining power. Two opposed actors are encoded (state-bar UPL enforcement bodies; equity partners as a faction); all 50 perspectives returned by the position-filtered dissent slices are cited and engaged or explicitly disposed in coverage, and the contested-topics contesters not otherwise retrieved are disposed by name. One coalition survives the joint-action test (the Claude for Legal integration bloc); two former coalitions were demoted to relationships. Positions are relative to AI-enabled restructuring of production, pricing and staffing; horizon statements are analyst estimates.
